items.title: Robustness Starts with the Objective: Designing and Certifying Robust LLM-Generated Heuristics
items.summary: LLMs are increasingly used to design heuristics for computer systems. However, most synthesis frameworks evaluate candidates by their average performance, which can mask severe regressions on specific workloads. Even adding adversarial training inputs doesn't eliminate these regressions, and percentile objectives (e.g., optimizing for the 95th percentile) overlook how severe regressions can be beyond the selected threshold. We present TAILOR, a framework that guides LLM synthesis using the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the cost difference between each candidate and an existing baseline on the same workload. This paired CVaR measures the average difference over the worst fraction of workloads. We show that a negative paired CVaR guarantees improvements in both average performance and tail optimality gap relative to the unknown optimum, without ever computing that optimum. We find that TAILOR achieves the best mean--tail trade-off among the synthesis objectives we evaluate across three case studies: Azure GPU batch admission, Azure VM packing, and server placement. Tested across seven diverse optimization benchmarks, TAILOR produces heuristics that are certified with 99% confidence to improve both average performance and tail optimality gaps over the baseline in six of them. On these six benchmarks, TAILOR also outperforms known robust, human-designed alternatives in the tail while achieving better or comparable average-performance improvement over the baseline.

items.title: From Confounding to Counterfactuals: A Cross-Layer Causal Model for RAN Scheduling
items.summary: Data-driven control in radio access networks (RANs) selects resource allocations using associations between control actions and key performance indicators (KPIs) learned from network telemetry. Because the shared radio environment influences both the scheduler's decisions and the resulting performance, a bias known as confounding, such associations overstate the effect of an allocation and misdirect resources toward user equipment (UEs) that cannot benefit. Moreover, individual UEs respond heterogeneously to the same decision, so even a corrected average effect does not identify which UEs gain from additional resources. While causal inference has recently been applied to RANs, existing approaches do not model the cross-layer mechanisms that connect an allocation to its outcome. In this paper, a hierarchical structural causal model (H-SCM) spanning the PHY, MAC, and network layers is proposed that separates cell-load confounding from UE-specific response heterogeneity. In particular, a counterfactual scheduling problem is formulated in which physical resource block (PRB) allocations are selected using per-UE counterfactual goodput rather than observational conditional averages. This problem is solved via a pipeline combining constrained causal discovery, structural-equation fitting, and abduction-action-prediction. Simulations demonstrate that naive observational estimation overstates the full-PRB response by 73.3%, whereas adjustment for cell-load confounding reduces the relative error to 9.8%. Held-out interventions are predicted with a coefficient of determination of 0.988. Counterfactual scheduling achieves a mean relative loss in total cell goodput below 0.5% against the ground-truth optimum, compared with 2.0-2.9% for a neural-network baseline.

items.title: When Shards Fly: Cross-Tensor In-Flight Conversion for Low-Latency, Low-Memory Weight Updates in Disaggregated RL
items.summary: Disaggregated LLM reinforcement learning (RL) repeatedly synchronizes policy weights between training and rollout GPU pools. Existing systems reduce communication through shard delivery and replica forwarding, yet separate conversion passes and staging buffers still add latency and GPU-memory overheads to synchronous updates. We present ShardFly, which coordinates reusable transfer planning with streaming GPU execution for synchronous, in-place weight updates. ShardFly introduces two components. The Planner compiles native shard mappings, quantization dependencies, and replica routes into cross-tensor schedules, reserving payload buffers only for scheduled transfers. The Executor runs each rank's schedule in one persistent transfer kernel, fusing memory-layout conversion, quantization, GPU-initiated communication, and destination writes while forwarding transformed bytes across replicas. Plans and communication state are reused under stable configurations and replaced between updates for coordinated rollout scaling. On up to 32 H20 GPUs, ShardFly achieves complete BF16 weight-update speedups of 1.26--27.92$\times$ across five models and four baselines: veRL NCCL, Awex, veRL NIXL, and WeightBridge. In end-to-end Qwen3-30B-A3B GRPO across four rollout configurations, ShardFly improves response-token throughput by 5.49--6.71\% over veRL NCCL.

items.title: Efficient Reconfigurable Architectures for Deep Learning
items.summary: The growing computational demands of deep learning (DL) have driven AI-optimized reconfigurable devices, such as the AMD Versal AI Engines (AIEs), the Intel Stratix 10 NX Tensor Blocks (TBs), and the AMD Ryzen AI NPUs. Their heterogeneous resources and novel dataflow models make efficient exploitation nontrivial, and FPGAs lack native support for structured sparsity. This dissertation optimizes dense general matrix multiplication (GEMM), the dominant DL kernel, on these devices, proposes FPGA architectural enhancements for structured sparsity, and extends the techniques to AMD Ryzen AI NPUs. First, MaxEVA optimizes GEMM on Versal AIEs, achieving up to 2.19$\times$ higher throughput and 20.4% higher energy efficiency than the state of the art. It is then extended to arbitrary matrix sizes, and a systematic framework is proposed for the Stratix 10 NX TBs. Both frameworks reach state-of-the-art int8 throughput of up to 77 and 68 TOPS, and energy efficiency of up to 0.94 and 1.35 TOPS/W, on Versal and Stratix, respectively. Next, Systolic Sparse Tensor slices (SSTs) are proposed as in-fabric hard blocks supporting dense, 2:4, 1:4, and a new 1:3 sparsity level. SST-based GEMM accelerators achieve up to 5$\times$ higher frequency and 10.9$\times$ lower area than conventional FPGA logic, and on sparse ViT and CNN models SSTs deliver up to 3.52$\times$ speedup over dense in-fabric acceleration with up to 13.3% area increase. Finally, a common systematic methodology is proposed to optimize GEMM across the XDNA and XDNA2 AMD NPUs, reaching state-of-the-art performance of up to 6.76 and 38.05 TOPS (int8) and 3.14 and 14.71 TOPS (bf16), respectively.

items.title: RAMA: Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent Routing with Episodic Memory for LEO Satellite Networks
items.summary: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks present a challenging routing environment due to rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) routing methods typically rely on current observations and information encoded in network weights, limiting their ability to exploit successful past experiences. We propose RAMA, a retrieval-augmented multi-agent DRL framework with Approximate Information State (AIS), in which each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, neighboring state information, and retrieved entries from a per-satellite episodic memory. Retrieved experiences are integrated through a Transformer-based decision network trained with AIS-based auxiliary objectives. With weights frozen in a 140-satellite Kepler constellation, RAMA reduces mean end-to-end latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% relative to the state-of-theart double deep Q-network (DDQN) routing method, mainly by avoiding long detours. Updated online, RAMA remains stable while DDQN degrades. On the 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1, the reduction in mean latency grows to 93.2%, and updating RAMA online lowers its mean latency by a further 25.5%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented memory for scalable decentralized routing in LEO satellite networks.

items.title: LLM Fine-Tuning Workloads: Characterization, Challenges, and Opportunities for Serverless AI
items.summary: Serverless execution of Large Language Models (LLMs) is becoming important, reflecting their wide societal use. An increasingly present stage in LLM pipelines is fine-tuning, which specializes trained models and improves inference performance. Serverless operation of LLM fine-tuning workloads shifts operational concerns from the user to the provider. For these new workloads, providers face important operational complexities, such as performance issues, resource waste, and even service failure due to misconfiguration. However, optimizing such workloads is still at an early stage, and, relevant to this work, relatively little is currently known about how LLM fine-tuning workloads run in practice. In this work, we address the knowledge gap by characterizing the execution of LLM fine-tuning workloads on clusters equipped with different GPUs, running LLM models at various scales. We analyze IBM's LLMFineTuningBench, a large-scale, diverse profiling dataset of 30,920 fine-tuning experiments that records both successful and failing configurations. We provide quantitative insight into throughput (expressed in tokens/s), scaling, failure, and potential for performance optimization for four commonly used GPU types, in setups of 1 to 32 GPUs. We find that (1) job feasibility (run or fail) depends on workload properties, with failure ratios rising from 52% for small batch sizes (16-64) up to 95% for the largest (1,024); (2) throughput grows logarithmically with batch size; (3) scaling is near-linear when the workload is deployed intra-node, and optimizations such as RoCE substantially improves efficiency for inter-node deployment (e.g., 0.72 vs. 0.26 efficiency without RoCE); and (4) system-level optimizations can outweigh application-level ones (RoCE, up to 2.9$\times$, vs. Fast MoE, 1.7$\times$).

items.title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation
items.summary: Real-time long-video generation requires continuous output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Existing chunk-wise autoregressive methods face challenges in both generation efficiency and long-video quality: serialized denoising and history-cache refresh require two forward passes even with one-step denoising, and longer rollouts can degrade quality and cause camera drift. We propose Wave Forcing (WF), which co-designs generation, training, and execution for continuous video output with multi-step denoising. WF uses chunk-wise causal attention to access earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising is complete, and distributes staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages across full-model replicas to achieve 1F1C: one output chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill. To adapt the model to this continuous generation process, we develop a three-stage training procedure that successively introduces mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history. To execute this process efficiently, Wave Runtime (WaveRT) uses Wave Parallelism (WP) for early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap, together with optimized kernels and pipelined VAE decoding. Experiments on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B show that 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing while achieving higher Dynamic Degree on both short and long videos. Our system efficiency experiments show that 4-step WF achieves 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding 7.07x the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. In DiT-only tests with matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, denoising steps, and GPU counts, WP delivers up to 2.53x the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B-14B).

items.title: FieldRT: Reconfigurable Architecture from Geometric Sensitivity to Streaming Acceleration
items.summary: Geometric perception on edge must simultaneously achieve two goals that are rarely addressed together: preserve accurate spatial understanding for object localization and operate within stringent latency, memory, energy, and precision constraints. This coupling is particularly evident in oriented bird's-eye-view (BEV) detection, where global context, multi-scale interactions, and geometric fusion affect both prediction quality and hardware dataflow. Conventional deployment flows first compress a model using aggregate quality or complexity proxies and then map the compressed operations to a fixed accelerator interface. This separation risks removing geometric structures that appear redundant under coarse metrics but are critical for precise localization, while leaving hardware-level efficiencies in the retained geometry unexploited. We present FieldRT, an algorithm-hardware co-design methodology that uses a common analysis of geometric sensitivity and data lifetime to derive both the deployment profile and its spatial realization. We deploy FieldRT with Axis-Fusion Network (AFN), a sub-million-parameter oriented-BEV detector, and construct controlled profiles that vary the capacity and organization of its geometric processing. The experiments show that redundancy is task-dependent rather than uniform across metrics. Dense prediction can improve while real instance detection deteriorates; coarse localization may remain stable while strict-IoU precision degrades. Moreover, transformations that are individually safe can become detrimental when combined. FieldRT translates the retained geometric structure into a parameterized streaming architecture that shares field access and storage across spatial operators. The resulting custom-PL primitives achieve production-scale numerical closure on an AMD Kria KV260 and make otherwise infeasible multi-dilation execution realizable.

items.title: ParaBlock++: Communication-Computation Parallel Blockwise Hierarchical Federated Learning
items.summary: In the emerging 6G paradigm, where AI-driven services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained infrastructures, the convergence of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++, a low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical federated learning (HFL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaboratively engage in federated learning (FL) via ground-satellite links (GSLs) supported by LEO satellite megaconstellations. Within this architecture, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through inter-satellite links (ISLs). Departing from conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ employs asynchronous BCD-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and non-convex objectives, and formulate optimization problems to determine optimal cluster resource allocation and model partitioning for minimizing global training latency. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for deep neural networks (DNNs) such as ResNet-18, offering promising directions for federated learning across geographically remote areas enabled by 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.

items.title: Route-Aware EM Surrogate for Automated LC Matching Network Optimization
items.summary: This paper proposes an open-source automated LC matching network optimization framework that combines schematic-level design optimization with electromagnetic (EM)-aware post-layout refinement. An ML-based surrogate predicts the frequency-dependent complex admittance of individual routes, enabling reuse across matching network topologies and physical layouts for the same technology node without retraining. These route models guide post-layout passive retuning to recover matching performance while preserving the layout footprint. Evaluated in a commercial 65nm CMOS technology, the surrogate achieves 1.94-4.91% mean absolute percentage error with respect to a full-wave electromagnetic solver, with no detected passivity violations. All designs meet matching targets under full-layout EM verification in optimization runtimes below 70s.

items.title: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Agentic LLM Serving
items.summary: Key-value (KV) caches impose substantial memory pressure on large language model serving systems, requiring cache eviction when capacity is insufficient. Existing mechanisms typically evict KV from the ends of cached sequences to preserve prefix sharing across requests. However, agent workloads repeatedly reuse long histories across successive turns. Recomputing the KV cache for tokens near the end of a sequence is substantially more expensive than for earlier tokens because their attention computation involves longer histories. To address this problem, we propose preserving shared prefixes and evicting the KV cache from the beginning of the remaining history while retaining the cached suffix. We build Penelope around this strategy by co-designing the eviction policy, KV recomputation, and unified GPU-CPU cache management. Returning requests reuse the KV cache retained in GPU or CPU memory and recompute only missing segments while preserving reuse of the cached suffix. We implement Penelope in SGLang and evaluate it on three Qwen3 model sizes using real agent traces. Compared with SGLang, Penelope reduces mean time to first token by up to 60% and job completion time by up to 37% with a GPU-only cache, and by up to 76% and 60% with a two-tier GPU-CPU cache.

items.title: Migrating a Legacy Scientific Application with an AI Coding Agent: NICAM from Fortran to Kokkos
items.summary: Migrating from Fortran to C++/Kokkos broadens access to hardware accelerators through backends such as CUDA and HIP while offering greater flexibility in software design. However, legacy Fortran applications often have large codebases, making manual porting time-consuming and costly. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and AI coding agents have made large-scale code migration increasingly feasible. In this study, we ported NICAM (Nonhydrostatic ICosahedral Atmospheric Model), a legacy Fortran climate model accelerated with OpenACC, to C++/Kokkos with the assistance of Claude Code. The agent translated the code directly from Fortran to C++/Kokkos under human review. Approximately 140,000 lines of Fortran were analyzed and ported into 35,000 lines of C++/Kokkos, covering the dynamical core and seven physics packages. A 100-member ensemble comparison with the original Fortran model showed that the port is statistically consistent with the original. Performance was evaluated on Miyabi-G, an NVIDIA GH200 cluster, and Sirius, an AMD MI300A cluster. Compared with the Fortran/OpenACC baseline on GH200, the port achieved application speedups of $1.71\times$ on GH200 and $1.54\times$ on MI300A. The CUDA build achieved a GPU kernel-time speedup of $1.38\times$ on GH200. After normalization by peak memory bandwidth, the HIP build on MI300A achieved $0.96\times$ the kernel performance of the Fortran/OpenACC baseline.

items.title: Matching Workloads to Blackwell: Power-Resolved Benchmarking of NVIDIA B200 and B300 across HPC and AI Workloads
items.summary: We evaluate NVIDIA B200 and B300 (Blackwell Ultra) GPUs on two independent eight-GPU clusters, spanning computer-vision inference and training, LLM inference with Llama-3-8B and 70B~\cite{llama3}, and six production HPC codes. Because our harness keeps inputs resident in device memory, a host-side data pipeline is excluded by construction, localizing the cause to per-kernel cost. Two B300 nodes of identical silicon differ by 2.1$\times$ in time-to-first-token solely from a development vLLM build. We give per-workload procurement guidance.

items.title: DeepWeave: Weaving Neural and Symbolic Evidence for ML-Based Network Intrusion Detection System
items.summary: Machine learning-based network intrusion detection systems can recognize complex traffic patterns, but often require substantial labelled attack data, degrade under deployment shift, and provide limited evidence for analysts. We present DeepWeave, a probabilistic neuro-symbolic Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) that makes logic an integral part of detection. DeepWeave automatically constructs and validates interpretable rules, represents neural predictions as probabilistic predicates, and reconciles both evidence sources through explicit coupling policies over packet-, flow-, and hybrid-views. The resulting proofs provide intrinsic explanations for rule-supported alerts. Across multiple datasets, DeepWeave improves low-data detection, false-positive control, transferability, and robustness. With only 50 labelled packet observations per attack class, it improves macro-F1 from 0.632 to 0.924 and reduces the attack false-positive rate from 0.075 to 0.008 over the matched neural baseline. Its proofs are also more stable than post-hoc neural attributions, while batched inference keeps probabilistic reasoning practical. These results demonstrate label-efficient, adaptable, and inspectable neuro-symbolic intrusion detection.

items.title: Online Autotuning of Algebraic Multigrid via Contextual Bandits and Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Algebraic multigrid (AMG) methods are widely used for solving large sparse linear systems, but their efficiency depends strongly on interacting setup and solve parameters. Effective parameter choices typically depend on the problem. A recursive LSTDQ controller uses residual and timing observations to estimate the AMG solve time within each attempt and adapt relaxation weights between multigrid cycles. Across grids of sizes $40^3$, $60^3$, and $80^3$, the joint autotuning method reduces total runtime, including recurring learner computation, by 36.1-43.3% for diffusion problems and 19.8-31.0% for diffusion-advection problems over sequences of 5000 linear systems, relative to the reference BoomerAMG default configuration. items.title: Zeroth-Order Policy Optimization for Scheduling in Queueing Networks
items.summary: Reinforcement learning in queueing network scheduling presents significant challenges because of the countably infinite state space and the high stochasticity in transitions. items.title: Autotuning GPU Thread Block Sizes for Large-Scale Stencil Applications Using the OPS DSL
items.summary: Large-scale structured-mesh stencil applications can run for hours or days on modern HPC GPU platforms, making launch-configuration choices important. OPS enables high-level stencil codes to target multiple GPU architectures, but its GPU backends rely on a default or user-selected global block/workgroup shape, even though different kernels, problem geometries, and architectures may favor different configurations. This paper presents a transparent per-kernel block/workgroup-shape autotuning extension for OPS. The extension explores valid block/workgroup shapes during execution, records the fastest configuration for each kernel, and enables precomputed replay of the selected configurations in subsequent runs. We evaluate the approach on structured-mesh proxy and academic research applications, covering 459 unique kernels across 3 NVIDIA and 2 AMD GPUs. The evaluation reports speedup distributions, representative wall-time summaries, timing variability, and input problem shape effects. Replaying the best per-kernel launch shapes improves 923 of 995 measured application/input/GPU cases over the default OPS shape. Depending on the GPU, the median speedup ranges from 1.02x to 1.18x, with individual configurations of LAPL2D, TTI3D, and OpenSBLI-based TGV solvers exceeding 1.5x. The results also show that performance sensitivity is not limited to launch shape. At fixed cell count, changing the input problem shape changes precomputed-replay runtime by 0.8-34.6% in representative cases, while kernel-level timing variability depends on the interaction between runtime contribution, input problem shape, and GPU/backend behavior. Overall, automatic per-kernel block/workgroup-shape selection improves OPS performance across GPUs, provided shape sensitivity and timing stability are interpreted together.

items.title: ORION: An Outcome-Driven LLM Advisor for RL-Based Multi-Domain 6G Slice Placement
items.summary: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. Experiments on a parametrized family of multi-domain topologies show that no fixed planning strategy dominates across all regimes: the performance ranking reverses between topology classes, and feasible placements exist for most rejected requests but remain undiscovered. These findings identify the plan layer as the decisive performance lever. We introduce ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and generate abstract placement plans. A cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, while per-domain agents place the functions. ORION main contribution lies at the plan layer: an outcome-driven episodic memory that records, for each completed attempt, the network-condition profile, the proposed plan, and its verified feasibility outcome. The memory feeds verified successes and labelled failures back to the planner, thereby closing the adaptation loop using deployment feasibility rather than a scalar reward assigned to the planner's own proposals. To isolate the effect of the plan quality, we evaluate the planner on held-out topology families while keeping the downstream selection and execution mechanisms fixed. Under this controlled setting, the proposed memory improves admission by $4.6$--$11.5$ percentage points over the same planner without memory, while importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.

items.title: RecIS: Unifying Sparse and Dense Computation for Efficient Recommendation Training
items.summary: Modern recommender models scale sparse representations and dense computation together. They process thousands of heterogeneous feature fields, long user-behavior sequences, and trillion-scale Embedding parameters, while their dense networks increasingly use large Transformer architectures. The resulting execution mismatch creates fine-grained operations within stages, load imbalance and synchronization delays across devices, and GPU resource bubbles between stages. As models grow, these costs become a primary limit to scalable recommender training. Although existing systems improve Embedding caching and data prefetching, these inefficiencies still coexist in the GPU-centric workloads we study and jointly limit end-to-end throughput. We present RecIS, a unified framework for GPU-centric recommender training. RecIS treats the complete path from input features to dense computation as one optimization target and coordinates three complementary mechanisms. First, adaptive fusion combines fragmented feature transformations with vectorized memory access. Second, a GPU Embedding engine uses hash-based sharding and hierarchical communication to balance request placement and eliminate redundant transfers; it also specializes aggregation for forward and backward index structures. Third, a multistage pipeline overlaps input preparation for future iterations with dense computation in the current iteration. Together, these mechanisms reorganize a fragmented sparse front end into a dataflow that continuously feeds dense computation. We evaluate RecIS on representative industrial recommender models across distributed training platforms. Compared with PICASSO and TorchRec, RecIS reaches up to $2.62\times$ and $1.15\times$ their throughput, respectively, while reducing step latency by up to 61.5\% and 12.9\%. RecIS provides an efficient and scalable training system for large recommender models.

items.title: Multistatic ISAC with Deep Learning-Based Clutter Suppression for 5G and Beyond
items.summary: Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) systems using 5G and beyond signals of opportunity enable joint wireless sensing and communication using shared infrastructure and spectrum resources. items.title: AuditFL: A Contract-Backed Clearing Layer for Open Federated Learning
items.summary: Federated learning (FL) keeps raw data local, but most deployments still rely on a trusted coordinator for client admission, checkpoint distribution, update collection, aggregation, and rewards. This paper presents AuditFL, a contract-backed clearing layer for auditable FL in open settings. AuditFL keeps training and aggregation off chain, stores model artifacts in an assumed reliable off-chain artifact store, and records only content identifiers and economic state on chain. Clients reserve update tickets with deposits, publish update identifiers, and later claim refunds or rewards; the task coordinator publishes global checkpoints and finalizes rounds through deterministic settlement rules. The design does not remove the aggregator, but makes its on-chain round decisions attributable, replayable, auditable, and economically constrained. We implement AuditFL as both a deterministic state-machine prototype and a Solidity contract on a local Ethereum-compatible Anvil chain. On full MNIST with Dirichlet non-IID splits, 12 rounds, and up to 200 clients, AuditFL preserves the Plain FL learning trajectory while its overhead follows closed-form control-plane models. At 200 clients, the contract run issues 5,026 transactions, stores 2,413 off-chain artifacts (144.9 MiB), and consumes 829.7M EVM gas, dominated by per-client reserve and publish calls. Controlled dropout, invalid-update, and artifact-unavailability stress tests reduce inclusion nearly linearly but still finalize rounds, with final-accuracy changes remaining within a few tenths of an accuracy percentage point even under high injected failure rates.

items.title: Randomized Caches in Hardware: Challenges and Trade-offs
items.summary: Randomized caches protect against side-channel attacks by obfuscating the mapping of memory addresses to cache locations. Existing proposals typically describe architectural behavior, leaving practical hardware implementation challenges largely unexplored. We implement four prominent designs, CEASER-S, ScatterCache, SassCache, and MIRAGE, and integrate them as the last-level cache (LLC) of a multi-core out-of-order RISC-V system-on-chip (SoC). We identify common and design-specific implementation challenges and develop practical solutions. We evaluate complete FPGA implementations by running SPEC CPU 2017 rate and GAPBS workloads to completion, providing, to our knowledge, the first comparative evaluation of these designs on a common full-system hardware platform. Pipelining the index derivation function (IDF) alone is insufficient: in three of the four variants, other components become the frequency bottleneck, reducing frequency by up to 35% relative to the baseline set-associative cache. Redesigning the critical paths while preserving mappings, rekeying, and victim-selection policies brings the three affected variants to no more than 10% below the baseline frequency, at the cost of added latency or reduced concurrency. Increased LLC access latency, rather than additional misses, dominates IPC degradation, reducing instructions per cycle by up to 5% for SPEC and 11% for GAPBS. Hardware overhead depends on the design and implementation technology: FPGA lookup-table usage increases by 10-35%, while ASIC area increases by 1-14%.

items.title: Falcons: Pushing the Speed-Ratio Limits of Lossy Compression for Parallel Scientific Applications
items.summary: The extreme volume of scientific data has become a critical challenge for modern exa-scale scientific computing applications, and error-bounded lossy compression remains indispensable for scientific data management due to its high data reduction rate and controllable data fidelity. However, to ensure sufficient data reduction, existing compressors incur prohibitive computational overheads in real-world parallel scientific computing applications. To overcome the performance bottlenecks of error-bounded lossy compression, we present \textbf{Falcons}, a broadly deployable error-bounded lossy compressor that simultaneously achieves \textbf{high compression ratios with ultra-fast throughput, minimizing the overhead in parallel scientific applications}. Falcons integrates three key designs: memory-regularized interpolation with SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data) vectorization, distribution-adaptive lossless coding, and application-oriented optimizations for multiple parallelization schemes. Across our evaluations on cutting-edge supercomputers, Falcons clearly outperforms state-of-the-art compressors, simultaneously achieving up to 29\% compression ratio improvement and 255\% throughput improvement. In case studies of real-world applications, Falcons accelerates large-scale parallel data I/O and remote transfer by up to 44.6\% and 51.5\%, and provides 1.55$\times$ end-to-end speedup for the full WRF (Weather Research \& Forecasting) application workflow.

items.title: Analysis of Triggered Packet Streams: Stochastic Bounds on System Time under General Triggering Delays
items.summary: Many emerging communication systems increasingly involve devices that transmit packets in multiple causally dependent stages as part of an internal workflow, rather than waiting for receiver feedback. To analyze such systems, we recently introduced the $\mathrm{M^T/G/1}$ queue, in which primary customers arrive according to an exogenous Poisson process, and each triggers a secondary customer to join the queue after an independent random delay, called the \textit{triggering delay}. Our prior heuristic approximations assume identical exponential service times, and our matrix-analytic framework assumes exponential triggering delays. However, no exact analysis is available when both distributions are general. In this paper, we derive stochastic bounds, in the usual stochastic order, on the system-time distribution of each customer class under general triggering-delay and service-time distributions. The service times within each primary--secondary pair may be generally dependent. Using sample-path coupling and level-crossing arguments, we show that the stationary workload is stochastically sandwiched between those of two classical queues: a two-class $\mathrm{M/G/1}$ queue with independent Poisson arrivals (lower bound), and a batch-arrival $\mathrm{M^{[2]}/G/1}$ queue where each primary--secondary pair arrives simultaneously (upper bound). Notably, these bounds do not depend on the triggering-delay distribution, and they are asymptotically tight in the sense that the stationary workload converges in distribution to that of the lower- and upper-bound queues as the triggering delays diverge to infinity and converge to zero in probability, respectively. We translate these workload bounds into system-time bounds for each customer class. Simulation experiments support these bounds.

items.title: AI in the EGI e-infrastructure -- Past experiences and future strategies
items.summary: The EGI Federation has provided federated e-infrastructure services to European and global science for over 15 years. We review EGI's early experiences with AI in the interTwin and iMagine Horizon Europe projects, which built digital twins in physics and environmental sciences and an image-analysis platform for aquatic research. We then examine how the AI landscape has changed since 2023 and argue that the focus of AI in science has shifted from model training to adapting and applying AI to specific domains, projects and questions. Building on these lessons, we present the AI strategy emerging from the EGI Federation Strategy 2026-2030, organised around three enablers: (1) an AI-ready infrastructure connecting compute, data and application resources across the continuum; (2) human skills to know what is possible with AI and how to implement it; and (3) trust, to run AI with confidence even in high-risk environments. We describe the projects implementing each enabler, including federated LLM inference, AI-ready data platforms and AI competence centres, and discuss a division of labour with EuroHPC's AI Factories, RAISE, research infrastructures and EOSC, in which EGI specialises in the customisation and long-term operation of AI for research.

items.title: Accelerating posterior sampling in Bayesian inverse problems with diffusion models: an online-offline perspective
items.summary: Bayesian inverse problems require both informative prior models and computationally feasible posterior inference. We organize methods by how they split cost between offline preparation and online inference, and compare their assumptions, advantages and limitations, with emphasis on computational speedups. items.title: Lower Bounds on Inference Complexity for Polyak-Ruppert Averaged Stochastic Gradient Descent
items.summary: In this paper, we establish sharp lower bounds for Gaussian approximation of Polyak-Ruppert averaged stochastic gradient descent with polynomially decreasing step sizes. For every fixed exponent $γ\in(1/2,1)$, a single one-dimensional smooth, strongly convex example has approximation error with the limiting variance of order $n^{1/2-γ}+n^{γ-1}$ in Kolmogorov and convex distances. This matches the existing upper bound throughout the range of $γ$. The nonlinear bias contributes $n^{1/2-γ}$ even when the Gaussian reference uses the finite linearized variance. We also derive a lower bound of order $n^{-(1-γ)/2}$ for the relative mean error of estimating the limiting variance from one SGD trajectory, uniformly over a scalar quadratic family. With the limiting variance known, achieving approximation error $\varepsilon$ on this example takes order $\varepsilon^{-4}$ iterations for the best choice $γ=3/4$. Achieving both Gaussian approximation and relative mean variance-estimation errors at most $\varepsilon$ uniformly over the model class requires at least order $\varepsilon^{-6}$ iterations for every fixed $γ$.

items.title: A Deterministic Commitment Rule over Unstructured DAGs for Optimistic Replication
items.summary: In optimistic replication protocols, each replica uses the local state to execute requests from its clients in a wait-free manner, without synchronizing with other replicas. The outcomes may be revised later, making optimistic protocols only eventually consistent. To compensate for this consistency loss, an additional commitment mechanism can be employed: an underlying atomic broadcast protocol that allows replicas to periodically agree on the evolution of the object state. In this paper, we introduce a simple framework for optimistic replication based on a causality DAG: every replica represents the object state via a causally ordered set of client operations. The framework incorporates a deterministic commitment rule that incurs virtually zero message overhead beyond the basic dissemination of submitted operations.

items.title: CAPER: Circuit-Aware Parameter-Efficient Reasoning in LLMs for Analog Verification
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate analog circuits, yet every netlist must also be verified. We propose LLMs as verification assistants for analog circuits that flag unmet specifications and reliability issues that appear under process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) variation. To this end, we introduce CAPER, a circuit-aware PEFT method that adds a small branch alongside LoRA to read each stage's properties from the LLM and combine them from the relevant stages. In deciding whether a feedback loop is negative, LoRA and a high-rank adapter stay at chance, whereas CAPER answers every test case correctly. For comparator latches, where 11 of 90 LLM-written designs that work under nominal conditions fail under PVT variation, CAPER likewise learns to flag such latent failures, while generic adapters stay near chance. items.title: MemX: Memory-Aware Automatic Parallelism for Cross-Vendor Heterogeneous GPU Training
items.summary: Cross-vendor heterogeneous GPU clusters are increasingly used for large-scale model training. However, their GPUs differ substantially in compute power, memory capacity, and interconnect characteristics. In this paper, we present MemX, a new memory-aware automatic parallelism system that jointly optimizes iteration time, peak memory usage, and cross-GPU memory balance. MemX consists of a weighted-product objective function, heterogeneous recomputation strategies, a minimal-set profiler, interpolation-based data augmentation, a dual-output XGBoost predictor, and a hash-signature prediction cache, in order to accelerate search of large-scale auto-parallel best configurations at lower cost. We implement MemX on Megatron-LM and evaluate it against four automatic parallelism baselines on two heterogeneous clusters. MemX achieves the lowest prediction Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 12.17% and is the only method that identifies the real Top-1 configuration under both time-based and memory-balance rankings. In terms of search cost and search space, MemX searches 31,240 configurations in 26.5 seconds, while an end-to-end profiling baseline is extrapolated to require about 17 days at the same scale. The simulation study that extends the measured 20-GPU data to 40-GPU and 60-GPU clusters further illustrates the effectiveness of MemX at larger scales.

items.title: Geometry of Confabulation and Refusal in Small Language Models
items.summary: Faced with an unanswerable question, small language models can either refuse or confabulate: confidently produce a wrong answer. Can the hidden state before the first generated token provide a clue? Can we flip confabulations into refusals? I introduce ConfabQA, a 784-item benchmark whose obscure-pre-cutoff category breaks the typical correctness/knowledge-cutoff confound and map the geometry of the hidden state with linear probes, a sparse autoencoder (SAE), and direct optimization of intervention directions. On Qwen3-1.7B and Gemma 2 2B the probe separates upcoming refusals from confabulations well beyond prompt features (+7.4/+16.3 pp); on Llama 3.2 3B the ConfabQA margin is within fold-to-fold spread, but a direct refusal probe on PopQA and TriviaQA recovers +18-25 pp. On Qwen I closely inspect three candidate directions for the refusal vector: probe-recovered, Qwen-Scope SAE feature, and directly optimized. Although the three directions are pairwise 50-81 degrees apart, a push at or below the state's own norm along any of them flips most confabulations into refusal openings dominated by the "As..." family. Forcing the opener without touching the hidden state yields the same one-in-three judged-refusal rate as any push. The opposite push collapses refusals mostly into confabulations, yet leaves originally correct answers intact, so the direction gates the opening speech act rather than the knowledge behind it. Confabulations do not resolve into a concentrated feature in a dictionary or a token signature on Qwen3-1.7B. Scoring every probe on the margin over the strongest of four prompt-feature baselines extracts the hidden state's own contribution. Correctness signal is model-dependent and portable only for Llama 3.2 3B: 81% of the probe's margin over test majority survives transfer between ConfabQA, PopQA, and TriviaQA. Benchmark, judge, and code are released.

items.title: Can Agentic AI Undermine Its Own Assurance Loop? Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance for Cognitive Network Digital Twins
items.summary: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Network Digital Twins (NDTs) are increasingly combined to form Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs) that translate operational intents into network changes and support closed-loop management. However, a network change may achieve its intended objective while disrupting the monitoring or recovery mechanisms needed for subsequent decisions. For example, a service may be rerouted while its latency-monitoring traffic continues along the original path, producing measurements that no longer reflect the service's performance. We propose Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance (CLDA), an assurance mechanism that augments agentic AI-enabled NDTs with dependency-aware validation. In our framework, an agentic AI planner generates and refines network plans, while the NDT evaluates the projected network outcomes of these plans. CLDA extends this analysis using a Loop Dependency Graph (LDG) that connects service requirements to monitoring mechanisms, forwarding paths, failure domains, and recovery prerequisites. CLDA projects candidate actions onto these dependencies, checks intermediate states of multistep plans, and supports deterministic make-before-break repairs using temporary monitoring mechanisms. Unlike the Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner, CLDA uses explicit, deterministic rules for assurance decisions and repair. We evaluate CLDA through controlled reconfigurations, a 240-trial LLM-based planning campaign, and live network execution. A separate synthetic study examines deterministic assurance scalability across network models representing up to 1,024 routers.

items.title: When 200 OK Is Not an Answer: Silent Fetch Failures in Agentic Web Content Acquisition
items.summary: Web agents and answer engines fetch pages at question time, and liveness checks of cited sources treat an HTTP 200 response as success. On the held-out test split, the reviewed sample lowers this estimate from 25.5% to 20.0%. 13.1% of the sites whose random-path probe was answered returned 200. items.title: Decentralized Dynamic Stable Matching
items.summary: We study decentralized computation of the player-optimal stable matching (POSM) with unannounced player arrivals and departures. Without a common clock, event information, or direct communication, players propose to arms and observe only their own accept/reject outcomes. Mismatch cost counts rounds when the realized matching differs from the current POSM. For known preferences, we give a deterministic polynomial-time self-calibrating protocol with cost $O(t_*+K^2\log T)$, improving the previous bound $O(T^{1-1/K}(\log T)^{2/K})$. Here $K$ is the number of arms, $t_*$ the last event time, and $T$ the horizon. Players use only local time and proposal outcomes, knowing neither $t_*$ nor $T$. For any nondecreasing, polynomial-time-computable $g(t)=Ω(t)$, the protocol achieves $O(g(t_*)+K^2N_g(T))$. Here $g$ governs recovery time, while $N_g(T)$ counts iterations of $t\mapsto t+g(t)$ below $T$, exposing a tradeoff between recovery time and asymptotic mismatch cost. Any randomized protocol with recovery scale $g(t)\ge1$ and sublinear asymptotic mismatch cost has worst-case expected cost $Ω(t_*+N_g(T))$. Thus, with $g(t)=t$, our protocol is optimal up to a $K^2$ factor among sublinear-cost protocols with $O(t_*)$ recovery time. For unknown preferences on both sides, each player and arm learns its preferences from its own observations after matching. We give a decentralized learning protocol with expected cost $O(t_*+K^4Δ_{\mathrm{min}}^{-2}\log T)$, where $Δ_{\mathrm{min}}$ measures preference gaps. A complementary static-setting lower bound adapted from the literature shows that the dependence on $T$ and $Δ_{\mathrm{min}}$ is tight.

items.title: Power Adjusting Games Under Block-Dependent Pool Payout Schemes
items.summary: Advanced power adjusting block withholding attacks such as PAW and T-PAW have been analyzed so far under a global-reset version of the proportional scheme (GRP), which is rarely used in practice. In this paper, we analyze T-PAW, which contains FAW and PAW as special cases, under the block-dependent payout schemes deployed in practice: Pay-Per-Last-N-Shares (PPLNS), round-based Proportional (PROP) and exponential-decay (EXP). We derive the revenue ratios analytically, by renewal arguments for PPLNS and through the stationary carry process of an open round for PROP and EXP. We further introduce Power Adjusting Hopping (PAH), where an adversary of any size adjusts its power allocation towards the pool according to the blockwork age of the round without withholding any block, and derive its revenue ratios under PROP and EXP. We show that GRP misestimates the T-PAW gain in a scheme-dependent direction: it overstates the gain under PROP up to an order of magnitude and understates it under EXP for the original slush decay rate. PROP is highly vulnerable to PAH, while EXP faces a trade-off: a slow decay invites PAH and a fast decay invites T-PAW. PPLNS is the least vulnerable scheme: it is immune to PAH and it mitigates, but does not eliminate, T-PAW. All analytical results are verified by Monte Carlo simulations.

items.title: TRIAGE: Reliability- and Load-Conditioned Escalation for Two-Tier LLM Serving with a Semantic Evidence Judge
items.summary: Two-tier LLM serving escalates selected requests from a small model to a large one, but prompt-based routers cannot see whether retrieved evidence supports an answer, and they treat the GPU cost of an escalation as constant. items.title: Self-Normalized Inference from Riemannian Stochastic Gradient Paths
items.summary: Riemannian stochastic gradient paths estimate constrained parameters, but confidence regions usually require estimating the Hessian and gradient-noise covariance. We develop self-normalized inference from one path by expressing retained iterates in a common random tangent space. items.title: Riemannian Newton Methods with Statistical Inference

items.title: Resource Locks and Fast Unlock for Shared Balances in Certificate-Based Payment Systems
items.summary: Certificate-based payment systems such as FastPay settle a payment with one round of signatures from a quorum of validators and avoid global ordering. The client collects the signatures, and validators never talk to each other. We observe that this client-driven design is complete only as long as no lock is ever undone. Each account has a single writer, a conflict can only come from that writer's own misbehavior, and the account stays locked as the penalty. Stablecoin payments routinely need balances that several accounts debit: treasuries, merchant pools, allowances and subscriptions. There, honest accounts race, locks must be undone, and a quorum certificate held privately by a client can be silently overridden. We prove that no unlock rule is safe in this setting unless certificate formation is visible to validators. We present a hybrid protocol. Personal accounts keep the client-driven FastPay path unchanged. A shared resource is a balance with its own version number and a set of authorized accounts. Transactions on shared resources are submitted to any validator and certified by a two-phase broadcast, ECHO then READY. The admission check requires both the sender's nonce and the resource's nonce to be free. Without contention, this path needs no consensus. When concurrent debits split the votes in any proportion, validators detect the split themselves, freeze the affected resource version, and resolve it with one agreement instance scoped to that version. Losing transactions return their sender nonce. We prove consistency, no overdraft, validity, finality and liveness. The protocol composes with the PDCC reconfiguration protocol.

items.title: Nearly-Optimal Time-Sample Trade-off in Consensus Dynamics
items.summary: How does the number of sampled opinions affect the time required to reach consensus in distributed consensus dynamics? We study the synchronous $h$-\textsf{Majority}, in which every node independently samples $h$ nodes uniformly at random with replacement in each round and adopts a most frequent sampled opinion, breaking ties uniformly at random. We show that $h$-\textsf{Majority} achieves the nearly-optimal trade-off between the sample size and the consensus time, among a broad class of consensus dynamics. In particular, we prove the following results. For every sample size $h \ge 3$ and for every initial configuration, we prove that the process reaches consensus with high probability within $\widetilde{O}\left(1+\min\left\{\frac{1}{\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\}},\frac{\sqrt{n}}{h}\right\}\right)$ rounds, where $n$ is the number of nodes and $p_{\max}$ is the largest initial fraction of nodes supporting any single opinion. This is the first bound on the consensus time for $h$-\textsf{Majority} that holds for every $h\ge3$ and every initial configuration. When the initially most popular opinion has a sufficiently large lead over every other opinion, we show that all nodes adopt this opinion with high probability within $O(\log n/\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\})$ rounds. We establish a matching lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors for any fixed update rule that treats all opinions symmetrically and that selects either a sampled opinion or the node's current opinion.

items.title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Task-Free Federated Continual Forecasting via Two-Tier Replay under Concept Drift
items.summary: Federated time-series forecasting is increasingly important in applications where temporal data are distributed across privacy-sensitive clients, such as environmental monitoring, smart cities, and industrial sensing. A central limitation of current continual-learning protocols is that they usually assume predefined task boundaries, whereas deployed forecasting systems receive an uninterrupted stream and must decide autonomously when adaptation is necessary. This paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in task-free federated forecasting under concept drift. We introduce a drift-aware continual-learning protocol in which each client monitors prediction-window RMSE, calibrates a robust median threshold from the offline base period, and triggers adaptation only after persistent degradation. To mitigate forgetting, we propose a TwoTierReplay mechanism that separates fixed offline representative memory from online memory. The offline tier preserves long-term knowledge learned during the base phase, while the online tier captures recent distributional changes after drift. Experiments on the Beijing Multi-Site Air- Quality dataset with 12 clients, three forecasting targets, and three horizons show that TwoTierReplay achieves the best stability-plasticity score in all nine target-horizon configurations. It improves over the strongest baseline by approximately 11.4%. These results suggest that explicit temporal structuring of replay memory is a practical and effective mechanism for task-free federated continual forecasting.

items.title: VeilFL: Two-Stage Accountability for Anonymous Federated Learning
items.summary: Anonymous credentials can hide which registered client participates in federated learning, but their unlinkability also makes repeated misconduct difficult to associate. We present VeilFL, a two-aggregator protocol that adds staged accountability to PINE (USENIX Security '24). Each submission binds two private PINE messages, a round-specific pseudonym, and a tracing pair to the same hidden credential secret. This design enables detection of duplicate submissions within a round without introducing a persistent identifier for normal participation. VeilFL implements accountability in two stages. After a confirmed duplicate or joint PINE rejection, a threshold tracing committee reveals a stable handle that links faults associated with the same credential. The client's registered identity is recoverable only after the public log records the requisite number of linked faults and a separate threshold committee authorizes identification. Accepted and unopened submissions remain unlinkable under the stated assumptions. This work establishes submission binding and duplicate detection, anonymity, fault non-frameability, controlled two-stage opening, and preservation of PINE's privacy and validity guarantees. In the prototype implementation, creating a submission requires a median of 2.11 ms, while verification requires 3.01 ms. Batch verification reduces the cost to 1.86 ms per submission for a batch of 1,000. The public part of each submission is 608 bytes, with 1,248 bytes of additional VeilFL protocol data across the two aggregator submissions. Each opening stage completes within 4.3 ms for the different committee configurations.

items.title: Model Sharing Bayesian Optimization for Mechanical Wi-Fi Antenna Control in Multi-Station Environments
items.summary: Some commercial Wi-Fi access points used in homes and offices have antennas whose orientations can be adjusted manually. However, selecting suitable orientations is difficult for non-expert users, particularly in indoor multipath environments where reflections and polarization effects complicate the relationship between antenna orientation and link quality. We investigate automatic mechanical antenna orientation control for uplink Wi-Fi communication when the set of active stations changes over time. Building on our previously developed antenna-control system, we propose a model-sharing Bayesian optimization (BO) framework that learns the log-capacity of each link using a separate Gaussian process regression (GPR) model. The framework reuses these models across active-station (STA) combinations and optimizes proportional fairness, equivalently maximizing the geometric mean of the active links' capacities. Exploiting the linearity of this objective in log-capacity, we also derive a upper confidence bound (UCB) acquisition function and its gradient. We evaluate the framework through simulations driven by measured channel capacities and experiments with a mechanical Wi-Fi antenna prototype. The results demonstrate that the proposed model-sharing BO achieves better optimization performance than independent state-specific optimization by reusing the models trained on previously observed links.

items.title: ProVe: Proposer-Verifier Decoding
items.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive (AR) language models by letting a small model draft tokens serially and a large model verify them in parallel. We reverse these roles. Starting from a standard AR checkpoint, we fine-tune the large model into a proposer that predicts a block of future tokens in a single forward pass, then use one additional forward pass to verify the proposed block. This gives ProVe, Proposer-Verifier decoding. The verifier can be a smaller AR model or the proposer itself; the latter gives ProVe-lossless, which reproduces the proposer's greedy AR decoding. Across six benchmarks with a 32B proposer, ProVe-lossless reaches 2.5x average AR throughput without training a separate draft head. With a small 3B verifier, ProVe reaches 2.7x average throughput at 2.6 accuracy points below AR on the six-task average, providing a controllable tradeoff between speed and accuracy.

items.title: Does Random Search Discover Task Experts? Revisiting Neural Thickets
items.summary: Pretrained models are typically viewed as generalists, requiring bespoke post-training to achieve task-specific expertise. Gan & Isola (2026) recently proposed a striking alternative: that pretrained models lie in a dense neural thicket of task specialists, which can be surfaced with simple Gaussian weight perturbations. We examine this neural thicket of task-specific experts and identify several key findings that question this perspective. First, we find that the apparent lift of the best-of-N selected perturbation decays quickly with selection-set size m, strongly suggesting overfitting to the selection questions. In fact, for 10 of the 12 model-task pairs we study, a simple null model of pure selection noise predicts more than 75 percent of the top expert's reward lift. Second, the top experts' advantage often vanishes on held-out questions or remains within the run-to-run variability of the unperturbed pretrained model. Third, we find that majority voting over the top-K selected perturbations, termed RandOpt(N, K) by Gan & Isola (2026), is often matched or outperformed by majority voting over K samples from the base model. Overall, our results suggest that random weight perturbations may be ineffective at uncovering task experts around pretrained models, and that task adaptation requires more sophistication than random search. Code and artifacts are available at github.com/asil012/RevisitingNeuralThickets.

items.title: Entropy-Regularized Reinforcement Learning for the Regime-Switching Consumption-Investment Problem
items.summary: This paper establishes an entropy-regularized reinforcement learning (ERRL) framework for the continuous-time consumption-investment problem under a regime-switching market model with general utility functions. Specifically, the optimal investment strategy follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution, whereas the optimal consumption strategy takes the form of a Gibbs measure---which specializes to a Gamma distribution under logarithmic utility and a non-standard exponential distribution under power utility. Crucially, our theoretical analysis reveals that the classical deterministic optimal decisions correspond to the mode---rather than the mean---of these exploratory distributions. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the exploratory value function to its classical unregularized counterpart as the temperature parameter vanishes. For algorithmic design, we develop a continuous-time q-learning framework grounded in a novel continuous-time q-function, prove the policy improvement theorem, and establish martingale characterizations for both on-policy and off-policy learning. We find that parameterizing the actor network based on theoretical distribution families can help accelerate convergence and enhance numerical stability. Furthermore, numerical experiments across regime-switching environments provide empirical support for our theoretical findings, demonstrating stable loss convergence as well as the monotonicity and concavity of the learned value functions.

items.title: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits
items.summary: Mitigating unfair disparities in sequential decision-making is a growing concern in machine learning. We study contextual bandits under a global covariate-based Lipschitz fairness constraint, pioneered by \cite{dwork2012fairness}, requiring individuals with similar contexts to receive similar action distributions. We show that this constraint induces a randomisation region near the decision boundary and explicitly quantify the population level cost of fairness. We further establish a canonical representation of the optimal fair policy, which reduces the fair policy design to a lower-dimensional boundary optimisation problem. We develop a lazy fair greedy algorithm that exploits fairness-induced covariate diversity under continuous contexts, with policy updates computed via finite-dimensional linear programming. For general context distributions, including discrete and mixed contexts, we propose a lazy polyhedral upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm, whose optimistic optimisation reduces to finitely many linear programs over confidence-set vertices. Both methods satisfy fairness at every round and achieve regret of order $O(\sqrt{T} + T^{(d-2)/(d-1)}{\indc\{d\geq 4\}})$ up to poly-logarithmic factors, where $d$ is the dimension of the contexts. A matching minimax lower bound for $\ell_1$-based fairness establishes optimality, and reveals an unavoidable nonparametric cost of learning the decision boundary, which dominates the parametric learning cost when $d \geq 4$. Experiments on synthetic and real data support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.

items.title: CuPH: Parallel Cubical Persistent Homology via Level-Synchronous Component Tracking
items.summary: Persistent homology (PH) is a mathematically principled multi-scale topological descriptor of shape and connectivity in data. It is widely applied in image classification, segmentation, and shape analysis across medical and aerial imaging, providing structural information that pixel-wise deep learning may overlook. Standard cubical PH decomposes an image into cubical cells (vertices, edges, and squares) and reduces them sequentially in filtration order. This sequential reduction has $Θ(n)$ parallel depth for an $n$-pixel image, limiting within-image GPU parallelism and constraining its use in topology-aware deep learning. We introduce CuPH, a GPU-based parallel algorithm for computing cubical PH on 2D images that operates directly on pixels rather than cubical cells. CuPH buckets pixels by filtration values, activates them with a level-synchronous sweep, and tracks connected components with a lock-free union-find method. We prove that CuPH produces persistence diagrams identical to standard cubical PH on integer inputs, with a stability bound for floating-point inputs. CuPH reduces parallel depth from $Θ(n)$ to $O(L\log n)$ for an image with $L$ intensity levels. We implement the level sweep as a single CUDA kernel, eliminating cross-level kernel-launch overhead. Empirically, CuPH is $18.6$--$99.6\times$ faster than the existing GPU baseline (CMP). As a drop-in PH backend, CuPH accelerates topology-aware classification ($4.2$--$16.7\times$) and segmentation ($8.3$--$44\times$) while preserving accuracy. It also enables computing full-image PH losses on high-resolution images, improving segmentation Dice by $2.2$--$4.6$ points over patch-local PH baselines and accelerating training by $25$--$31\times$.

items.title: Learning momenta for Hamiltonian-based models
items.summary: There has been increasing interest in methodologies that incorporate physics priors into neural network architectures to enhance their modeling capabilities. Among these methodologies, Hamiltonian neural networks (HNNs) and their variants have gained considerable attention. These architectures explicitly encode Hamiltonian mechanics both in their structure and loss function, resulting in desirable properties and additional modeled information. A crucial limitation of HNNs is their reliance on data on the target system's generalized momenta. This severely hampers their applicability when the analytical form of the generalized momenta is unknown, which frequently is the case in real-world applications. The goal of the present work is to develop a general extension of Hamiltonian-based architectures that addresses this issue by simultaneously learning the system's generalized momenta, Hamiltonian structure, and dynamics from data. The proposed architecture learns the generalized momenta when their analytical form is unknown, and only (potentially non-sequential) data on the state and its derivatives is available. A dissipative mass-spring system, a double pendulum, and a rolling disk under nonholonomic constraints are considered as canonical examples to assess the performance of the proposed architecture.

items.title: On Sparse Graph Limits for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
items.summary: Graph neural networks are often trained on small graphs and deployed on larger ones, raising the question of which graph information must be preserved for combinatorial optimization values to transfer across sizes. We establish size-transfer guarantees for normalized graph optimization values using finite collections of energy features. For affine objectives, including MAX-CUT, coloring defect, and independent-set density, differences in task value are controlled by discrepancies in normalized scalar energy probes on all bounded-degree graphs. For general Lipschitz objectives, such as those with balance penalties, an additional representation error appears; this error vanishes on hyperfinite graph families but can remain bounded away from zero on expanders. Thus, at fixed degree bound, state space, Lipschitz constant, and target accuracy, a finite energy representation independent of graph size suffices universally for affine tasks and asymptotically for general Lipschitz tasks on hyperfinite families. These results yield prediction guarantees under explicit conditions on encoder accuracy, readout stability, and representation coverage, together with statistical generalization bounds. Theoretically, we prove Shapley-Folkman bounds with sharp parameter dependence, including a dimension-free $\ell_2$ regime, and realize the resulting energy features with a fixed-weight message-passing network using random node initialization on bounded-treewidth graphs. Experiments with exact solvers and trained models test the resulting transfer guarantees.

items.title: Energy-Efficient Geographic Multicast Routing in Cognitive Wireless Sensor Networks
items.summary: Energy consumption is a major design concern in wireless sensor networks. Cognitive radio provides opportunistic access to licensed spectrum, while multicast routing allows several destinations to share forwarding paths. In this paper, we propose two geographic multicast routing protocols for cognitive wireless sensor networks, CCast and PCast. CCast combines multicast-tree construction with a latency-oriented spectrum-selection metric. PCast uses a normalized link-power cost to select routes and can avoid regions where primary users occupy lower-frequency bands. Both protocols use local neighbor information and destination coordinates, without requiring a complete network-topology map. Simulations compare the proposed protocols with geographic multicast routing (GMP) and multiple unicast routing. In simulations, CCast and PCast reduce energy consumption by 21\% and 26\% relative to GMP, at the cost of longer per-destination routes and higher delivery delay.

items.title: LiHA: Worse is Better for Lightweight Hash-based Source Authentication
items.summary: The omission of source IP authentication remains a fundamental vulnerability in the Internet. Existing approaches rely on routing plausibility, topology assumptions, per-flow state, or wide deployment. These requirements have kept strong source authentication out of the data plane. As simplicity is the key to deployability, we present LiHA, a lightweight source authentication mechanism built around operations that routers already perform efficiently. LiHA binds secret keys to source prefixes using longest prefix match and authenticates each packet with a single message authentication code (MAC). The data plane requires no handshakes, per-flow state, or per-packet control plane access. A sender performs one prefix lookup and one fixed-size hash. The verifier repeats the same operations and forwards the packet only if the MAC matches. LiHA is designed for incremental deployment. It primarily protects against off-path attackers that spoof source prefixes they do not control. An on-path attacker can replay valid authenticated packets until the key rotates. LiHA does not eliminate every denial-of-service threat. Instead, it confines accepted traffic to authenticated source prefix space within participating networks. We argue that simpler source authentication with clear limits is more likely to be deployed. We implemented LiHA in three environments: as a set of user-space libraries, as eBPF programs, and in an FPGA. We found that the user-space implementation had very high overheads. The eBPF implementation got reasonable single thread performance even with a software based cryptographic hash. We found that only the FPGA could obtain 100 Gbps single thread performance, but that was only when bypassing the kernel using a DPDK user-level networking stack.

items.title: mmWave UE Positioning Under Blockage: Limits for ISAC-Assisted Handover
items.summary: Proactive handover can save a millimeter-wave (mmWave) link before a passing body blocks it, but only if the network knows where the user is. We ask whether the radio units that serve a user can localize it accurately enough from its uplink sounding reference signals. We derive position error bounds that include synchronization and array calibration errors, with and without reflected paths known from a digital twin, and test two estimators in a ray-traced street canyon on held-out scenarios. Three findings stand out. First, with line of sight to both radio units, array calibration, not bandwidth, limits the bound. Second, blockage degrades the line-of-sight-only bound sharply, whereas known reflections keep the map-aided bound low. Third, a simple dominant-path estimator fails where it matters most: its errors grow sharply around blockage, and proactive handover becomes worse than the 3GPP baseline. A map-aided multipath tracker cuts the median error from 12 to 3.7 cm and removes this significant penalty at link margins of 15 dB and above, but does not yet beat the baseline.

items.title: Sense Less, Miss Less: Evidence-Driven Sensing Schedules for ISAC
items.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) lets a base station detect human motion with the same signals it uses for data, but every sensing transmission takes resources from users. Sensing rarely while nothing moves saves resources, yet a brief hand gesture by an otherwise still person can then start and end between two transmissions and go unnoticed. We propose an evidence-driven schedule, based on data-efficient cumulative-sum (CuSum) change detection, that pauses sensing while measurements indicate no motion and senses continuously once they suggest motion. It is adapted to orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) sensing, where requests can be blocked by data traffic and measurements arrive late, and evaluated with an articulated human model of limb motion. In simulations without wall reflections, with the same monitoring budget and below one false alarm per minute, it detects 1.5--4.2 times as many limb movements within 200~ms as periodic sensing. A tuned two-rate trigger performs similarly, and the gain over periodic sensing persists, without retuning or cost matching, in a simulated room with wall reflections. Under a small budget, measurements should decide when to sense.

items.title: 6G-Enabled Cooperative Connected and Automated Mobility: Are We There Yet?
items.summary: Connected, cooperative, and automated mobility (CCAM) is a key enabler of future intelligent transportation systems, requiring seamless integration of communication, sensing, computing, and automation technologies. This paper surveys the state of the art in CCAM, focusing on key use cases and performance indicators, enabling technologies, system architectures, and standardization and regulatory developments relevant to large-scale deployment. Particular attention is given to cooperative perception, collective awareness, artificial intelligence and machine learning as fundamental building blocks of future CCAM ecosystems. The paper further identifies major research challenges related to scalability, interoperability, and real-time operation in highly dynamic mobile environments. Finally, it outlines future research directions toward achieving large-scale, safe, and resilient CCAM systems supported by next-generation communication networks.

items.title: Adaptive Optimizers Can Get a Policy Ranking Wrong: Momentum, Dependent Data, and a Two-Run Remedy
items.summary: Operators choosing among decision rules, such as when a battery charges or where an idle taxi goes, rank them by estimated long-run value. A standard estimator, linear temporal-difference (TD) learning, fits values from one stream of correlated observations. Large fits often use an adaptive optimizer, such as adaptive moment estimation (Adam), with fixed averaging rates. We show that these rates can change what is estimated, not just how fast: the same observations drive the updates and the optimizer's step-size scaling, moving the fit away from the intended TD value. The shift differs across rules, so it need not cancel in a comparison, and more data only makes a wrong ranking look more certain. Our remedy refits the same data at a second averaging rate that halves the effective gain, the number to which the leading shift is proportional. Twice the new fit minus the original removes that shift. In New York taxi and battery models calibrated to real data, common optimizer settings leave the selected rule unchanged but order close rules wrongly and misstate its value. Our remedy corrects nearly every wrong ordering, with one extra fit when the shift is moderate and two when it is larger.

items.title: Do Earnings Calls Help Predict Financial Restatements? Evaluating Text Beyond Public Firm Information
items.summary: Financial restatements correct errors in previously published financial reports. Could managers' language in earnings calls warn of them in advance? Comparing 109 calls that precede restatements with 218 matched control calls, we find that the text predicts restatements but adds no detectable ranking gain beyond public firm information. A text classifier beats chance, largely because of restatements tied to special-purpose acquisition companies, but a model using only public information scores slightly higher. With refitting, the 95% interval for the gain from adding text (-0.05 to 0.11 AUROC) still leaves room for a meaningful benefit. A large language model scores higher, but we show that it names the exact ticker in 66% of masked transcripts, and it was released after the restatements occurred. Our results suggest that finding new warning signs in call text requires a public-information baseline and a check of what a language model already knows.
